In 2009, Dakota Meyer drove straight into an ambush in Afghanistan's Ganjgal Valley, again and again, to pull out wounded men and recover the fallen. His actions were credited with saving 13 Americans and 23 Afghan troops, and in 2011 he received the Medal of Honor, the nation's highest award for valor. Now the Marine has been handed a very different kind of mission: making sure the troops who serve today have a decent place to sleep at night.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has named Meyer a senior advisor to the Pentagon's Barracks Task Force. The job is simple and hands-on. Meyer will travel the country, base to base, walking through barracks, talking with the service members who live in them, and flagging what needs to be fixed. His first stops are in California this week, Camp Pendleton, then Twentynine Palms and Miramar, and if the schedule holds he'll have inspected around 21 bases by the end of December.

The problem he's being sent to tackle is real and long-running. Government watchdogs have reported for years that many enlisted troops live in substandard barracks, some with serious health and safety issues. An August 2026 report put the military's installation maintenance backlog at an estimated 285 billion dollars. Hegseth has called the living conditions "unacceptable," and the task force, formed in late 2025, is meant to set department-wide standards and steer money toward the worst of it.

Some of that money is already moving. A major 2025 defense funding law set aside roughly 1.2 billion dollars for barracks improvements, including a dedicated Marine Corps "Barracks 2030" effort and funds to restore and modernize housing across the Army, Navy, Air Force, and Space Force. Recent projects include new and modernized housing at bases in Georgia and Washington state.

What makes this one land is who's carrying it, and why. Meyer knows exactly what these troops give, because he gave it himself. "They shouldn't have to fight for basic living conditions when they come home at night," he said. And he's putting his own name on the outcome: "If we don't get this fixed, there's only one person to blame. Me." For the men and women living in those rooms, having a Medal of Honor Marine show up in person to see the state of them is about as strong a signal as the Pentagon can send that someone is finally paying attention.

Are you a robot? Or are you lethal?

In the high-stakes environments where our service members operate, grit and readiness are the only verifications that matter.

Most countries don't offer to pay for someone else's military base. Poland is doing exactly that. It has been pushing hard for a permanent U.S. base on its territory, and it has put billions of its own dollars on the table to make it happen.

Poland formally requested a new permanent American base in June 2026, and the talks have moved quickly since. Polish President Karol Nawrocki has gone as far as calling the base "confirmed," and U.S. officials have said there's been "major progress." That said, Washington has not announced a final decision, and no location has been named yet, so the deal isn't signed, it's close, according to the Polish side.

The part that stands out is who pays. Poland has signaled it is willing to cover much of the cost itself. Polish officials have put their share at more than 15 billion zloty, roughly 3.4 billion euros, and a Bloomberg report placed the figure as high as 4.4 billion dollars. For a country that sits directly on the border with Russia's Kaliningrad territory and with Belarus, a permanent American presence is clearly worth paying for.

The base would likely house a full brigade, somewhere between 3,000 and 5,000 U.S. troops, with Poland's deputy defense minister calling 4,500 the most realistic number. Over time, Poland would like to see as many as 15,000 American troops in the country. Right now, roughly 6,500 to 7,000 rotate through on a non-permanent basis.

Plenty is still undecided, the exact location, the final cost split, even the name (Poland's president has floated calling it "Fort Trump"). But the direction is clear, and it's unusual. In a long-running debate about whether America's allies pay their fair share, Poland isn't asking the U.S. to spend more. It's offering to spend its own money to keep American troops close.

This is what lethality in motion looks like.

The M142 HIMARS doesn't just participate in the fight, it dictates the terms.

📸 Army Sgt. Steve Asfall

NATO is being tested along its southeastern edge, and this week the alliance is meeting to decide what to do about it. Over the weekend, Romanian F-16 fighter jets intercepted and downed two drones that had crossed into the country's airspace from the Black Sea.

What stands out is how routine this is becoming. Romania says it has recorded 35 unauthorized drone incursions so far in 2026, compared with 9 in all of 2025, and has downed six of them this year after downing none the year before. The defense ministry identified the latest two as Geran-type attack drones flying at around 280 mph, a design associated with Russia's arsenal, though officials have not formally blamed Russia for this specific incident.

The response is moving up to the alliance level. NATO's governing body, the North Atlantic Council, is set to meet in Brussels, and Romania's foreign minister said the talks will focus on expanding NATO's presence in the Black Sea region and increasing surveillance. Bulgaria, which shares the same coastline, has asked allies for additional aircraft and counter-drone equipment.

The incursions come as the war in neighboring Ukraine continues to brush up against NATO's borders. The alliance's secretary general, Mark Rutte, met Romanian and Bulgarian leaders the week before and said NATO had strengthened its posture along its eastern flank.

None of this points to a wider war. Most of these drones appear to be strays or probes rather than deliberate strikes on NATO itself. But the numbers are climbing fast, and the alliance is being forced to work out, in real time, how to defend a long stretch of coastline against cheap drones without overreacting to every one that wanders across the line. That problem isn't going away.
The Army must return to its original purpose: controlling and securing land, which is fundamental to human flourishing and fulfillment.
